idiom_name: opaque struct + const function-pointer table + public wrapper functions
implementation_notes: C has no classes, so both interfaces are built by hand: the type is an opaque struct (forward-declared in the header, defined only in the .c file) whose layout starts with a pointer to a const table of function pointers - that table is the subclass interface, and the header exposes only wrapper functions that validate, lock or account before dispatching through it. File-system code in the Linux kernel is exactly this shape: vfs_read() checks the file mode, access_ok() and rw_verify_area() accounting, then calls file->f_op->read (or read_iter). Keep one static const table per concrete type, install a complete table in the constructor, and never expose the table to callers.
pitfalls: A NULL or partially initialised function-pointer table turns every wrapper call into a crash: install a complete table in each constructor and reject construction otherwise.
The wrapper and the table entry must agree on the explicit self parameter and calling convention; a mismatch is undefined behaviour, not a compile error.
Nothing stops a caller from casting the opaque pointer and reaching the table directly - keep the struct definition out of installed headers and treat the guarantee as a header discipline.
